title: Labeled break and continue
body: C# 15 ships with .NET 11, whose release candidates carry a go-live licence; general availability is expected in November 2026. These examples are checked with SDK 11.0.100-rc.2. Details can still change before release, so re-check the What's new page after GA.

Stage 1 noted that `break` and `continue` affect only the innermost loop, so leaving nested loops needed a flag, a `goto` or an extracted method. C# 15 lets them name a label on an enclosing loop or switch: `continue outer;` starts the next iteration of the loop labelled `outer`, and `break outer;` leaves it.

Put the label directly on the loop statement it names (`outer: for (...)`). Without a label, `break` and `continue` keep their old meaning. The IDE0410 style rule suggests labeled jumps where code uses the flag or `goto` workarounds.
Labeled jumps help in searches over grids or nested collections and in parsers that skip ahead. Very deep nesting is still a sign that extracting a method with `return` might read better.
Check that the label names the loop you mean; `continue outer` re-evaluates the outer loop's condition and increment, which is easy to forget when the outer loop also maintains state.
challenge: Given lines of comma-separated numbers, sum each line but skip the whole line (continue to the next line) as soon as a non-number appears, using a labeled continue. Lines: "1,2,3", "4,x,5", "6".
question: What does `continue outer;` do inside a nested loop in C# 15?
correct: Starts the next iteration of the loop labelled outer
wrong: Restarts the inner loop from its first element
Jumps to the statement after the outer loop
reasoning: A labeled continue targets the named enclosing loop; break outer would leave it instead.
